---
name: actana-sessions
description: Drive Actana Control Cores and Sessions with the `actana` CLI — register and select a Core, see which Harnesses it can run, start Sessions with a prompt, wait for them to settle, collect the report each one wrote, send follow-up input, and stop them. Use when asked to run work in one or more Sessions, to provision several Sessions at once ("give me three sessions, each on a different thing"), to check on or collect results from Sessions already running, or whenever a task would be done by another agent on a Core rather than here.
x-actana-managed: true
---

# Driving Cores and Sessions with `actana`

`actana` is a client. A **Core** is a machine running the Actana Control daemon;
a **Session** is one Harness process — a vendor's coding agent — running on that
Core in the Core's workspace (`~`). There are no Projects (ADR 0041). Sessions
belong to the Core, not to this command: a Session keeps running after `actana`
exits, and any later `actana` invocation can list it, read it, write to it or
stop it.

If `actana` is not on this machine, or reports no Core, say so and stop. Do not
install anything and do not guess at a Core's address.

**This skill is invoke-only, and the one installed beside it is not. The
asymmetry is deliberate — do not tidy it into symmetry.** This one sits
installed and does not volunteer: it is for a Session whose operator has asked
for work to be run in other Sessions. Its sibling, the sub-agent skill, is
**eager**: it triggers on a prompt telling a Session that it is acting as a
sub-agent of an orchestrating Session, and this skill is what teaches you to put
that declaration in every prompt you send. The two roles have opposite trigger
requirements — one is a thing an operator asks for, the other is a thing a
Session is *told it already is* by the prompt that woke it — and one
`description` field cannot hold both. That, and nothing about length or
tidiness, is why there are two files.

## Orientation, in the order that answers the questions

```bash
actana core ls                 # Cores this machine can reach; * marks the selected one
actana core use <name>         # select one for subsequent commands
actana harness ls --json       # what the selected Core can actually run, right now
actana session ls --json       # Sessions already running there
```

`--core <name>` overrides the selection for a single command. Every list verb
takes `--json`, and under `--json` only the JSON document reaches stdout —
diagnostics go to stderr — so parsing is safe.

**On a machine that is itself a Core, that Core is already registered and
already selected.** Installing a Core wires it to the same machine's `actana`,
so `core ls` lists it and it is what every command below means unless `--core`
or `core use` says otherwise. Address it by default; do not ask the operator to
pair the machine you are already standing on.

**Pick the Harness from what `harness ls` reports, every time.** It lists each
Harness with a `status` of `available` or `missing`; only `available` can run.
There is no default and no preference order here on purpose — operators have
their own, this skill has none, and a Harness that was available yesterday may
be missing today. Ask the operator if the choice matters to them and nothing in
the request settles it.

## Starting one Session

```bash
actana session start "<prompt>"            # prints the session id, exits
actana session start "<prompt>" --json     # the same as an object
actana session start - < brief.md          # a prompt of `-` is read from stdin
```

Useful flags: `--harness <id>` (one of the ids `harness ls` printed),
`--title <text>` (what it is called in a listing), `--dangerously-skip-permissions`
(run the Harness without permission prompts — only when the operator has asked
for unattended work). Every Session starts in the Core's home (`~`); there is no
`--cwd` and no Project argument.

`start` returns as soon as the Core has the Session running. The prompt is
delivered by the Core, which watches the Harness boot and types when it is
ready; add no delays, no leading newline and no "press enter" of your own.

**Running is not the same fact as ready to be sent to.** The Harness is spawned
when `start` returns; it takes the prompt seconds later, once its composer is
up. A `session send` in between goes into a terminal that is not reading and is
discarded — along with the starting prompt queued behind it, so one impatient
line loses two messages. If the next thing you do is `send`, start with
`--await-prompt`:

```bash
ID=$(actana session start "<prompt>" --await-prompt)   # blocks until it landed
actana session send "$ID" "<follow-up>" --enter --wait --json --wait-timeout 1800
```

It blocks only until the Core reports the prompt delivered — seconds on a warm
Harness, not the length of a turn — prints the id as usual, and **exits non-zero
unless the Core positively confirms the prompt went into a composer it saw**.
That covers the prompt it gave up on, and it also covers a Harness whose composer
the Core does not yet recognise, where the prompt was typed on a quiet screen
that may have been a trust dialog. A start that cannot establish readiness says
so rather than reporting success; the message names what stopped it. `session
resume <id> "<prompt>"` takes it too.

`--wait` is the longer wait and cannot be combined with `--await-prompt`, and
`--wait-timeout` does not apply to it: the Core bounds that wait itself. The two
do not report quite the same thing: `--wait` reports a prompt the Core **gave
up on**, and reports `promptDelivered` as whatever the Core said while it
waited — never from the absence of a report. Without either, `--json` answers
`promptDelivered: null`: nobody adjudicated it. `null` is also what you get when
a Harness exits before the Core decides. Treat it as "not known".

**`--harness` is how one round spans several Harnesses.** Nothing else is
needed for it: each `session start` takes its own `--harness`, so a round of
lanes on different Harnesses is a round of ordinary starts. Pick every id out of
what `harness ls --json` reported as `available`, and never out of memory.

## Waiting, and reading the result

A Session hands work back by **writing a report file** into the Core's Shared
folder (`~/shared` on the Core), and `actana` learns that it landed from the
Shared folder's watcher. Nothing in that path goes through a screen, a renderer,
a replay ring or a scrollback limit, and a Session's status does not decide it.
A transcript is what a human reads over somebody's shoulder; **a result is a
file**.

```bash
ID=$(actana session start "<prompt>")                   # prints the id, exits
actana session wait "$ID" --wait-timeout 900            # blocks until the report lands; prints its path
actana shared get "sessions/$ID/report-1.md"            # read it
```

`wait` settles when the report file is there **and its last line is exactly
`ACT-REPORT-END`**. A report that landed before you started waiting settles it
at once. With `--json` it prints one object: `sessionId`, `turn`, `reportPath`,
`waited`, `settled` and the `report` text itself. `--wait-timeout <seconds>`
bounds the wait; without it the wait has no deadline of its own. A timeout is
this side giving up, not a verdict about the Session: it is still running on the
Core and can still be listed, read from and stopped. A Session that never writes
a report runs out the timeout, and that is how a lane that produced nothing
shows up.

While a Session is alive — which is what the `live` field on its
`actana session ls --json` row tells you, and the only thing that does — you can
also look at it directly:

```bash
actana session logs <id>          # the transcript, rendered, while the harness is running
actana session send <id> "text"   # write into it, with the report block, and press Enter
actana session wait <id>          # block until a turn's report lands
actana session kill <id>          # stop the harness running for it
```

`actana events tail --json` follows the Core's event log as NDJSON if you want
to watch state change rather than poll. `logs`, `events tail` and `session ls`
are for **watching progress**; none of them tells you a report is ready. The file
does.

## The multi-turn loop

A Session is a conversation, not a single question. The whole loop:

```bash
ID=$(actana session start "<first prompt>")
actana session wait "$ID" --wait-timeout 900                       # turn 1: report-1.md
actana session send "$ID" "<follow-up>" --enter --wait --wait-timeout 900   # turn 2: report-2.md
actana session send "$ID" "<next>" --enter --wait --json                    # turn 3: report-3.md
```

**Every turn gets its own report file**, and the turn number in the filename
keeps them apart, so turn 2 can never be read as turn 1's report. The starting
prompt is turn 1. `send` takes the next turn after the reports already there
(never 1) and prints which one that is; with `--wait` it then waits for exactly
that file, through the watcher, from a cursor taken *before* it wrote, so a
report that lands at once is not missed.

- **`send` presses Enter by default**, as a second write after the text, so the turn
  starts. `--enter` is still accepted and changes nothing on a send that carries
  text. `--no-enter` types the text and sends no return, which starts no turn — so
  it cannot be combined with `--wait`.
- **`wait <id>` with no `--turn` means the latest report there is** — one still
  being written, or the last complete one. After a `send` that did not wait,
  name the turn it printed: `actana session wait <id> --turn 2`. Without
  `--turn` the answer would be the previous turn's report.
- **To answer a Harness that stopped to ask** (a permission or trust dialog, a
  choice), use `actana session send <id> 1 --enter --no-block`: the text is typed
  exactly as given, with no report block, no turn and no Shared folder. That is
  not a turn, so there is no report to wait for.
- **Two sends in a row before either reports** would both take the same turn.
  Wait for the first, or give each its own `--turn`.
- **A timeout is this side giving up, not a status.** The Session is still
  running on the Core, and `session logs`, another `session wait` and
  `session kill` all still work.

## The report contract

The paths are the Core's, relative to the Shared folder (`~/shared` on the
Core; `actana shared` takes the Shared-relative form):

| What | Path |
| --- | --- |
| a plain Session turn | `sessions/<session-id>/report-<turn>.md` |
| a Task's result | `tasks/<task-id>/success.md`, `fail.md` or `partial-<n>.md` |
| a Task's log of one attempt | `tasks/<task-id>/attempt-<n>.log` |
| an older result, after a re-run | renamed to `attempt-<n>-<name>`, for example `attempt-1-success.md` |

- **The final line of a report is exactly `ACT-REPORT-END`.** That is the
  completeness proof and **the only thing that settles a turn**. Not a status,
  not an event, not a timeout. Only the last non-blank line counts: the marker
  quoted inside a fenced block, in a diff or in the middle of the file is not a
  finished report.
- **You do not tell the Session any of this.** The Core appends a standard block
  to every starting prompt it delivers, and `session send` appends the same block
  to every follow-up. The block says that the Session's workspace is its home
  directory, that `~/shared` is shared with the operator and syncs within seconds,
  where this turn's report goes and that it ends with the marker, and not to use
  sudo. Say what the work is, in whatever detail it needs, and nothing about the
  mechanism.
- **Do not name a path of your own.** The path comes from the Session's id and the
  turn, so there is nothing to mint and no two lanes can collide. A report path
  you invent is a file nobody is watching.
- **A Session started with no prompt gets no block**, so it has been told no
  path. Send it a prompt with `send`, which carries the block.

Then say what the Session is to do, and open with the declaration that turns the
sub-agent skill on at the other end:

> You are acting as a sub-agent of an orchestrating Session. <the work>

**That first sentence is not a courtesy.** The sub-agent skill installed on that
Core is eager and triggers on exactly that declaration, so a prompt without it
wakes a Session that does not know it must not start Sessions of its own. Send it
in **every** prompt you send, follow-up turns included.

## Reading a report

`actana shared` reads and lists the Shared folder through the Core, with no
terminal and no command run on the Core:

```bash
actana shared get sessions/<id>/report-1.md                  # to stdout
actana shared get sessions/<id>/report-1.md ./api-report.md     # to a local file
actana shared ls sessions/<id>/                              # what the Session has written
actana shared watch --json                                   # the folder's changes, as they happen
actana shared get --core <name> sessions/<id>/report-1.md    # on another Core
```

**Save a report you mean to keep to local disk** — give every lane its own local
filename, because "three Sessions, each on a different thing" is three reports
that you will want side by side. The file stays in the Shared folder: a turn's
report is never overwritten by the next turn's, and there is nothing to delete
before or after reading it.

## Files in the Core's home folder

`actana files` reads and writes the Core's own home folder (`~`, the Session's workspace)
through the Core, with no terminal and no command run on the Core. A path is relative to
the home; a path ending in `/` is a folder. It is for the work itself — a file a Session
should read, or a result file it wrote — and **not** for reports, which are read with
`actana shared` (above): a report lives in the Shared folder.

```bash
actana files ls src/ --depth 2                # the workspace, folders first
actana files get src/app.ts ./app.ts          # to a local file (stdout when none is given)
actana files put notes/brief.md ./brief.md    # create or replace; missing folders are created
actana files rm scratch/                      # a path ending in / deletes the folder
actana files ls --core <name>                 # the home of another Core
```

## `await.sh`, which waits for a whole round

This skill folder ships `await.sh` beside this file. It waits for **every lane at
once** — a per-lane wait serialises a round, so a six-lane round runs at the speed
of its worst lane *summed* rather than its worst lane alone — and each lane is
`actana session wait`, so each one settles on its report file through the
watcher, and then saves that report to local disk with `actana shared get`.

```bash
bash await.sh --out ./reports --timeout 1800 7f3a 9c1b:2
```

A lane is `<session-id>` or `<session-id>:<turn>`; with no turn it means the
latest report, as `session wait` does. `--core <name>` passes through to every
call, and `--kill` stops each Session once its report is safely on this disk. It
exits 0 when every lane's report was saved and 1 when any lane's was not, and
prints one line per lane saying which.

It is installed without an executable bit, on purpose — run it as `bash
await.sh`.

## Several Sessions at once

There is no batch verb. Provisioning N Sessions is N `session start` calls, and
that is deliberate: each one gets its own prompt and its own Harness, and a
Session that fails to start is one failure rather than a failed batch.

The shape that works:

1. **Ask what is missing before starting anything.** How many Sessions and what
   each one is for. If the operator said "three sessions, each focusing on three
   different things", the three things are theirs to name — do not invent a
   split and do not start work on a guess.
2. **Check `harness ls` once**, and use only `available` ids.
3. **Start every lane** with the sub-agent declaration in its prompt. Each report
   path follows from the Session's id, so there is nothing to mint up front:

   ```bash
   actana session start "$prompt_a" --harness "$h_a" --json > a.json
   actana session start "$prompt_b" --harness "$h_b" --json > b.json
   actana session start "$prompt_c" --harness "$h_c" --json > c.json
   ```

   Do not use `--wait` here: `start` returns as soon as the Core has the Session
   running, so three starts in a row are three Sessions working side by side.
   Take each `sessionId` out of its object.
4. **Wait for the files.** One call over every outstanding lane — `bash await.sh
   <id> <id> <id>` is that call — settles each lane on its own report and saves
   it down as it lands. A lane that has not finished costs a lane that has
   nothing.
5. **`logs`, `events tail` and `session ls` are for watching progress, and that
   is all they are for.** A row's `live` field says whether the harness process
   is still up and its transcript still exists; neither a terminal status nor
   `live: true` is a result. The result is the file. If a lane's wait runs out and
   no report file ever appeared, that is a lane that produced nothing — report it
   as exactly that.
6. **Report per Session, by id**, including the ones that produced no report. A
   Session that finished without one is a fact, not a gap to fill in.

**How many to start is the operator's decision, not a rule.** Every Session is a
Harness process on somebody's machine costing somebody's tokens. Start the
number that was asked for; if no number was asked for, ask.

**One level, and one only.** The Sessions you start are sub-agents, and the
skill they wake with forbids them starting Sessions of their own. Recursive
provisioning is unbounded — each level multiplies and nothing caps depth or
breadth — so the round you are running is the whole tree.

## When something is wrong

- **`no Core registered` / nothing from `core ls`** — this machine has no Core
  of its own and has not been pointed at a remote one. Pairing a remote Core is
  the operator's to do (`actana core pair`, with a code from `actana pair new`
  on the Core); say so rather than attempting it.
  Note that a machine running a Core registers it automatically, so an empty
  `core ls` means there is no local Core either — not that somebody forgot to
  pair one.
- **`harness ls` shows everything `missing`** — the Core has no coding agent
  installed. `actana harness install <id>` asks the Core to install one and
  waits for its verdict; it takes minutes and can legitimately fail.
- **`could not reach the Shared folder`** — the Core does not keep one, or the
  link to it failed. `wait` and `send` need it: the report is how a turn ends.
  `actana core status` says what this Core announces.
- **The report file never appears** — the wait runs out its timeout. Read the
  transcript with `actana session logs <id>` while the row still says
  `live: true`, and `actana shared ls sessions/<id>/` for what was written
  instead, and find out what the Session did. The usual cause is a Session that
  was never given the block (one started with no prompt), or a harness that
  wrote the file somewhere other than the path the block named. `send` it again
  as a follow-up turn, which names a fresh path; do not reuse the one that
  failed.
- **A report file is there but its last line is something else** — it is not
  finished. That is not an error and not a reason to read it: the wait keeps
  watching, and the timeout is what gives up.
- **`session logs` says the Session has no harness running** — the Harness has
  exited and its transcript is gone with it. Nothing recovers a transcript. A
  report file that was written survives it, which is the point of writing one.
- **A prompt seems not to have arrived** — do not retype it and do not send a
  bare carriage return. Delivery is the Core's job; a lost prompt is a bug to
  report with the Session's id, not a thing to work around from here.
actana-sessions.await.sh:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# x-actana-managed: true
#
# Wait for several Sessions' reports at once, save each one locally, and say per
# Session what happened.
#
# The marker on line 2 is the same marker `SKILL.md` carries in its frontmatter,
# and it means the same thing: this file was written by `actana` and `actana`
# will replace it, edits and all. Delete that line and this copy becomes yours —
# the installer reads the marker as a substring of a file's first bytes rather
# than through a YAML parser, so the escape hatch works here exactly as it works
# on the markdown.
#
# Run it with `bash await.sh` — it is installed without an executable bit, on
# purpose. The installer's whole safety argument is that it is a filesystem
# write and nothing else, and a write that also flips a permission bit is a
# larger act for no gain.
#
#   bash await.sh --out ./reports 7f3a 9c1b:2
#
# ── What it does, and what it leaves to `actana` ─────────────────────────────
#
# A turn is over when its report file is in the Core's Shared folder and its last
# line is exactly `ACT-REPORT-END`. `actana session wait` settles on exactly that,
# through the Shared watcher, so each lane here is one `session wait`, and this
# script does not look at the file, tail it or poll it itself. Three things are
# its own:
#
#  1. **Every Session waits at once.** A per-Session wait serialises the round: a
#     slow lane blocks fast ones that finished minutes ago, and a six-lane round
#     then runs at the speed of its worst lane *summed* rather than its worst lane
#     alone. The lanes run side by side and are collected together.
#  2. **Save locally before touching the Session.** The report is copied down with
#     `actana shared get` and confirmed non-empty on this disk before `--kill`
#     stops anything.
#  3. **Every lane gets its own local name.** "Three Sessions, each on a different
#     thing" gives every Session a report of the same shape; the Session id
#     prefixes the file so two lanes never overwrite each other.
#
# ── What it needs ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#
# `actana` on PATH and a Core selected (or `--core <name>`).

set -uo pipefail

OUT_DIR="."
TIMEOUT=1800
KILL_AFTER=0
CORE_ARGS=()

usage() {
  cat <<'USAGE'
bash await.sh [options] <lane>...

  lane            <session-id> or <session-id>:<turn>
                  with no turn, the latest report there is, as
                  `actana session wait <session-id>` means it

  --out <dir>     where saved reports land. Default: .
  --timeout <s>   give up on a lane after this long. Default: 1800
  --kill          kill each Session once its report is safely on this disk
  --core <name>   which Core, passed through to every `actana` call
  -h, --help      this

Exits 0 when every lane's report was saved, 1 when any lane was not.
USAGE
}

LANE_SESSION=()
LANE_TURN=()
LANE_LOCAL=()

# A value-taking flag with nothing after it is an error, and has to be said out
# loud. `shift 2` with one argument left shifts nothing and returns non-zero;
# nothing reads that status, so the same branch matched forever and the script
# hung with no output — a symptom indistinguishable from waiting on a Session
# that is still working. The caller here is a model composing a command line,
# and a silent hang is the worst thing it can be handed.
need_value() {
  # $1 is the flag; $2 is how many arguments are still unparsed, this one
  # included. Counting is the check: `${2:-}` would turn a missing operand into
  # an empty string, which is what hid this in the first place.
  [ "$2" -ge 2 ] && return 0
  echo "await.sh: $1 needs a value" >&2
  usage >&2
  exit 2
}

while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --out) need_value "$1" "$#"; OUT_DIR="$2"; shift 2 ;;
    --timeout) need_value "$1" "$#"; TIMEOUT="$2"; shift 2 ;;
    --core) need_value "$1" "$#"; CORE_ARGS=(--core "$2"); shift 2 ;;
    --kill) KILL_AFTER=1; shift ;;
    -h|--help) usage; exit 0 ;;
    --) shift; break ;;
    -*) echo "await.sh: unknown option \"$1\"" >&2; usage >&2; exit 2 ;;
    *) break ;;
  esac
done

if [ $# -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "await.sh: name at least one lane — <session-id> or <session-id>:<turn>" >&2
  usage >&2
  exit 2
fi

for lane in "$@"; do
  session="${lane%%:*}"
  turn=""
  [ "$session" = "$lane" ] || turn="${lane#*:}"
  if [ -z "$session" ]; then
    echo "await.sh: \"$lane\" is not <session-id> or <session-id>:<turn>" >&2
    exit 2
  fi
  if [ "$session" != "$lane" ]; then
    case "$turn" in
      ''|*[!0-9]*|0*)
        echo "await.sh: \"$lane\" has a turn that is not a number from 1" >&2
        exit 2
        ;;
    esac
  fi
  LANE_SESSION+=("$session")
  LANE_TURN+=("$turn")
  # The file name carries the Session id, because the report's own name does not
  # identify a lane: every Session's first report is `report-1.md`.
  safe_session="$(printf '%s' "$session" | tr -c 'A-Za-z0-9._-' '_')"
  LANE_LOCAL+=("$OUT_DIR/${safe_session}-report${turn:+-$turn}.md")
done

# Two lanes that would be saved under one name would overwrite each other, and
# under --kill the second save would destroy a Session whose report was already
# lost. Refused here, before a single Session is touched.
for i in "${!LANE_LOCAL[@]}"; do
  for j in "${!LANE_LOCAL[@]}"; do
    [ "$i" -lt "$j" ] || continue
    [ "${LANE_LOCAL[$i]}" = "${LANE_LOCAL[$j]}" ] || continue
    echo "await.sh: ${LANE_SESSION[$i]} and ${LANE_SESSION[$j]} would both be saved as" >&2
    echo "  ${LANE_LOCAL[$i]}" >&2
    echo "Name each lane once, or give them a --out directory each." >&2
    exit 2
  done
done

mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR" || exit 1
STATE_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" || exit 1
trap 'rm -rf "$STATE_DIR"' EXIT

# One lane: wait on the report through the watcher, then save it. Writes its
# verdict to $STATE_DIR so the round can be reported together.
run_lane() {
  local index="$1" session turn local_path report_path
  session="${LANE_SESSION[$index]}"
  turn="${LANE_TURN[$index]}"
  local_path="${LANE_LOCAL[$index]}"

  local wait_args=(session wait "$session" --wait-timeout "$TIMEOUT")
  [ -n "$turn" ] && wait_args+=(--turn "$turn")

  # stdout is the report's path in the Shared folder; stderr is for a person.
  if ! report_path="$(actana "${CORE_ARGS[@]+"${CORE_ARGS[@]}"}" "${wait_args[@]}" 2>"$STATE_DIR/$index.err")"; then
    printf 'failed\n' >"$STATE_DIR/$index.state"
    printf '%s\n' "$(awk 'END { print }' "$STATE_DIR/$index.err")" >"$STATE_DIR/$index.note"
    return
  fi

  # Save first. The Session is not touched until the bytes are on this disk and
  # the file we wrote is non-empty.
  if ! actana "${CORE_ARGS[@]+"${CORE_ARGS[@]}"}" shared get "$report_path" "$local_path" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    printf 'failed\n' >"$STATE_DIR/$index.state"
    printf 'the report landed (%s) but could not be copied down — it is still in the Shared folder\n' "$report_path" >"$STATE_DIR/$index.note"
    return
  fi
  if [ ! -s "$local_path" ]; then
    printf 'failed\n' >"$STATE_DIR/$index.state"
    printf 'the copy landed empty — the report is still in the Shared folder, nothing was killed\n' >"$STATE_DIR/$index.note"
    return
  fi

  printf 'saved\n' >"$STATE_DIR/$index.state"
  printf '%s\n' "$local_path" >"$STATE_DIR/$index.note"

  if [ "$KILL_AFTER" -eq 1 ]; then
    if actana "${CORE_ARGS[@]+"${CORE_ARGS[@]}"}" session kill "$session" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      printf '%s (Session killed)\n' "$local_path" >"$STATE_DIR/$index.note"
    else
      printf '%s (saved; the Session would not stop — kill it by hand)\n' "$local_path" >"$STATE_DIR/$index.note"
    fi
  fi
}

echo "await.sh: waiting for ${#LANE_SESSION[@]} lane(s)" >&2

# Lesson 1. Every lane at once, then collect them all.
for index in "${!LANE_SESSION[@]}"; do
  run_lane "$index" &
done
wait

failures=0
for index in "${!LANE_SESSION[@]}"; do
  state="$(cat "$STATE_DIR/$index.state" 2>/dev/null || echo failed)"
  note="$(cat "$STATE_DIR/$index.note" 2>/dev/null || echo "no verdict was written")"
  printf '%s\t%s\t%s\n' "${LANE_SESSION[$index]}" "$state" "$note"
  [ "$state" = "saved" ] || failures=$((failures + 1))
done

# A lane that produced nothing is a fact to report, not a gap to fill in.
exit $([ "$failures" -eq 0 ] && echo 0 || echo 1)

# Reporting back as a sub-agent

A prompt has told this Session that it is acting as a **sub-agent** of an
orchestrating Session, or ends with the Actana standard block that names a report
file. Either is what turned this skill on, and it means one concrete thing: the
Session that woke you is waiting on a **file** in the shared folder, not on your
screen, and it cannot see anything you print.

**This skill is eager, and the one installed beside it — the orchestrator skill
— is invoke-only. The asymmetry is deliberate; do not tidy it into symmetry.**
The orchestrator role is a thing an operator asks for, so that skill waits to
be asked. The sub-agent role is a thing a Session is *told it already is*, by
the prompt that woke it, and there is no operator in that loop to ask. One
`description` field cannot hold both requirements, which is why these are two
files.

**This skill covers two things and nothing else: the report file, and the
prohibition below.** It says nothing about how to do the work — not the
planning, not the implementation, not the testing, not what to put in the
report. That silence is deliberate and it is a bound, not an omission. An
orchestrating Session routinely passes other skills in the same prompt, and
this one is eager while those were invoked: advice from here would fight them
and would win. Whatever the prompt asked for, and whatever skill it named, is
what governs the work. This governs only how the answer gets back.

## The report file

- **The path is the one the standard block names, and the block is at the end of
  the prompt.** For a plain Session turn it reads
  `~/shared/sessions/<session-id>/report-<turn>.md` — under your home directory,
  in the `shared` folder, which is shared with the operator and syncs within
  seconds. Create the folders on the way if they are not there. Write it exactly
  where the block said, and do not helpfully move it somewhere tidier: the
  Session that woke you watches that path, and a file at a different place is a
  file nobody collects.
- **Use exactly the path the latest block gave you.** **Never invent one, never
  shorten one, and never reuse a path from an earlier turn** — the name carries a
  turn number precisely so that turn 2 cannot be read as turn 1's report. If a
  turn's prompt carries no block and names no path, say so in the Session and
  write nothing rather than guessing at a name nobody is watching.
- **A Task names its own folder instead**, `~/shared/tasks/<task-id>/`. In it,
  write `success.md` when the task is done, `fail.md` when it failed and
  `partial-<n>.md` when only part of it was done; the log of your attempt goes
  to `attempt-<n>.log`. If the task runs again, the older results have been
  renamed `attempt-<n>-<name>` already — leave them as they are.
- **The file's final line must be exactly `ACT-REPORT-END`**, on its own line,
  with nothing after it. That goes for every result file of a Task too.

That last line is the whole settling signal. The Session waiting on you is told
by the shared folder's watcher that the file changed, reads it, and compares its
**last** line to that marker: no status, no event and no timeout tells it you are
done, and nothing else will. Two consequences, and both of them bite:

- **Write the file only when the report is complete.** A file whose last line is
  anything else reads as "still working", which is correct while you are — but a
  half-written file left behind by an abandoned attempt is a lane that never
  settles.
- **Print nothing that matters only to the screen.** Whatever you say in the
  Session is read by a person, if anybody reads it at all. The file is the
  answer.

Do not write to a temporary name and rename it into place. It is better
engineering and worse instruction-following: the second step is the one that
gets skipped, and a temporary file that never lands is a lane that never
settles. One file, written once, ending in the marker.

## Do not create Sessions

**This applies when the prompt told you that you are a sub-agent of an
orchestrating Session.** A Session with only the standard block, started by an
operator, is the operator's to direct.

**A sub-agent must not start Sessions of its own through the `actana` CLI.** Not
on this Core, not on another one, not for a piece of the work that would divide
neatly. `actana session start` is the orchestrating Session's to call and not
yours. If the work genuinely needs more Sessions, say so in your report and let
the Session that woke you decide.

The bound is recursion. Every level of provisioning multiplies the level below
it, nothing caps the depth or the breadth of that, and every Session is a
harness process costing somebody's tokens on somebody's machine. One
orchestrating Session, one level of sub-agents.

**This does not restrict a harness's own native sub-agent facility.** If the
coding agent you are running inside has an in-process task or sub-agent
mechanism of its own, it stays available and this skill has nothing to say about
it: that is a different mechanism with different bounds, and it provisions
nothing on any Core. The prohibition is about `actana session start`, and about
nothing else.
